title: The Woodpecker's Doors
creature: A woodpecker who opens doors in trees
summary: Nils gets in easily. Getting out is a separate arrangement.

chapters.title: The Holes at Eye Height
chapters.text: A black woodpecker makes a nest hole about eight metres up and shaped like a keyhole, and there are forty or fifty of them in the Bjurholm forest and Nils could show you every one. The doors are different. They are at eye height — his eye height, and his father's, and his grandmother's, which is a range of about thirty centimetres and which is the first thing about them that does not make sense. Nils measured all nine at fourteen, with a tape, because he had got tired of people saying *about eye height* as though that meant anything. The lowest is a hundred and forty-one centimetres and the highest is a hundred and seventy-two. His grandmother's eye, at the time, was a hundred and forty-eight. His own is a hundred and seventy-nine and he has to stoop for every single one of them, which he did not expect and which annoyed him for about a year. They are round and they are the width of a fist and they go straight in, and there are nine of them in about four hundred hectares. They are always in a living tree. Never a snag, never a stump, never anything rotten. Four of the nine are in spruce, which no woodpecker in Sweden would bother with, and one is in a birch that Nils's father says has been there since the war. That is the part a forester notices first. Woodpeckers go for dead and dying wood because dead wood is soft and full of what they eat, and a healthy spruce is the last thing on the list — hard, resinous, and empty. There is also no woodpecker in that forest that makes a round hole a fist wide at a metre and a half. The great spotted makes a smaller one higher up. The black makes a bigger one, oval, at eight metres. Nils has looked this up in three books and has never found a species that would account for a single one of the nine. And you can look in. That is the whole of it and it is not much to say out loud. You put your eye to a hole in a tree and you look, and you see the inside of the tree. Not a hollow. There is no hollow; if you put a stick in, the stick goes in about four centimetres and stops on solid wood, and Nils has done this and can confirm it and has felt extremely stupid doing it. What you see, with your eye against the bark, is the wood from inside — the whole cylinder of it, going away from you in both directions, and every ring lit from somewhere and stacked outward from the middle in the order they were made. It is lit. He does not know from where and neither did his grandmother and there is no light source anywhere in a tree. What there is is enough of it to see by, evenly, with no shadows and no direction, in the way that a page in a book is lit when you are not thinking about the lamp. You are looking at the years.

chapters.title: What Is In There
chapters.text: Nils's grandmother taught him to read them, over about two summers, in the way she taught everything, which was by standing behind him saying nothing until he asked a question worth answering. The first question he asked that she thought was worth answering was, at eight, why the rings on one side were wider than on the other. She said that the tree grows more on the side that has more light and that this is called reaction wood and that if he wanted to know which way was south in that forest without a compass he could look at a stump. The rings are not labelled. Nothing tells you what year you are looking at. But they are not all alike, and once you can see the differences you can work outwards from the bark, which is now, and count. A wide pale ring is a good summer. A narrow dark one is a bad one. There are two rings in the birch that are so thin they are almost a line, and those are 1867 and 1868, and every tree of that age in northern Sweden has them and every forester in that country knows what they are. There is a black band in the pine by the marsh at about the sixtieth ring in and it goes right round, and that is fire. And there is one, in the big spruce at the top of the ridge, about a hundred and twenty rings in, where the wood on one side goes suddenly thick and buckled for four or five years and then settles down — which means that in about 1904 something took the top off that tree, or leaned another tree against it, and it spent five years correcting and then got on with its life. Nils could find that one in the dark by his fifteenth birthday. His grandmother had a name for it — *det stygga året*, the bad year — and Nils has never found anybody else in Västerbotten who uses that phrase and suspects she made it up. None of this is magic. He wants that established. Everything he has described is in the wood of every tree in that forest and you can see all of it by cutting one down and looking at the stump, which foresters do every day of the week. The only strange part is that you can see it from outside, through a hole the width of a fist, in a tree that is standing up and alive and has another two hundred years in it.

chapters.title: The Arrangement About Getting Out
chapters.text: The rule in the Bjurholm forest is that you do not look alone. Nils's grandmother gave it to him at eight, at the second door, on the day she first let him put his eye to one, and she gave it in a way that was not a warning and was not really an instruction either. She said: "Getting in is easy. Getting out is a separate arrangement, and I am the arrangement." He did not understand and she did not explain, and she stood behind him with a hand on his shoulder while he looked, and after a while she said his name and he stood back. He asked how long he had been looking. He asked because his legs had gone and because the light had changed and because there was a mosquito bite on his neck that had not been there. She said eleven minutes. He had thought it was somewhere under one, and he said so, and his grandmother said, "Yes," and they walked home. She did this eleven or twelve times over the next two summers and every time she told him the true number afterwards and every time it was between six and twenty minutes, and every time Nils would have sworn on anything that it had been about forty seconds. He tried counting once, at eleven, on the theory that if he counted seconds he would have a check on it. He got to about thirty and then found that he had stopped counting at some point he could not identify, and when his grandmother said his name he was on thirty-one and had been at the tree for fourteen minutes. That is the whole of the phenomenon and Nils has never found a way to make it sound serious. He knows exactly how it sounds. It sounds like being absorbed in something — like reading, like a screen, like the thing that happens to every human being who has ever been interested in anything. He thought that himself, at twelve, and was quite pleased with the thought, and said it to his grandmother. She said: "Try it in the dark." He went out that November at four in the afternoon with a head torch, to the third door, and he looked in, and his father came and got him at ten past seven. His father was not pleased and Nils has never blamed him. It was minus eleven and Nils had been standing still against a tree for three hours in a jacket meant for walking, and his father had gone out on the snowmobile at half six having tried the phone eleven times, and there had been a real and entirely ordinary danger in it that had nothing to do with anything strange. That is the argument Nils's father has always made about the doors and it is a good one: the interesting thing is not the tree, the interesting thing is a boy standing still in the dark in November.

chapters.title: Alone
chapters.text: He went alone at thirteen and he did it on purpose and there is no version of the story in which he did not know exactly what he was doing. It was the second week of June, which in that part of Sweden means the light does not go, and he told his sister he was walking to the ridge and he took a phone and a bottle of water and he went to the big spruce with the buckled rings. He wanted to see 1904 from the inside and find out what had happened. That was the whole ambition and he thinks now that it was a reasonable one. There is a hundred and twenty-first ring in that tree that goes wrong on one side, and Nils had a theory involving a windthrow in the neighbouring stand, and he had worked out that if he could see the buckling properly he could tell which direction it had come from. His sister found him at twenty past four in the afternoon. She was sixteen and had not wanted to come out and had spent the walk composing what she was going to say to him. She had come out at about three because he had not answered his phone and had not come back for lunch, and it took her the best part of an hour to find the tree, and when she got there he was standing with his forehead against the bark and his hand flat on the trunk beside him and he did not respond to his name the first two times. He had been there since half past nine in the morning. He was not hurt. He was not cold, in June. He had drunk none of the water. He had, by his own account, been looking for something in the region of ten minutes, and had been about to stop. His sister did not tell their parents and Nils has never known whether that was the right call. What she did was hit him, once, hard, on the arm, which he has always thought was fair, and then sit down on the moss and cry for a while, which he had not expected at all and which is the part he thinks about. He sat down next to her and did not say anything useful. He was thirteen and had nothing available except *I'm fine*, which he said about four times and which was true and which was not the point, and it took him until roughly his twenties to work out what the point had been. She had walked into a clearing and found her brother standing against a tree not answering to his name. Whatever was or was not happening inside that spruce, what she had was fifteen seconds of not knowing, and nothing that happened afterwards took those back. He is thirty-one. He works in the forest, which surprises nobody. He does thinnings and windthrow clearance and he has taken down perhaps eleven thousand trees, which he does not find difficult and which people always expect him to. He looks perhaps four times a year and he has never gone alone again, and the arrangement is now his sister, who lives in Umeå and who drives up for it, and who has never once suggested that they stop. He never did work out 1904. He can see the buckling perfectly well and it is the direction he expected, and there is a hundred and twenty-first ring in a living spruce on a ridge in Västerbotten that has an answer in it and does not have a question, and Nils has come to think that this is true of most of what is in there.
